Chapel Hill, North Carolina

Akshat Arora

Hi, I'm Akshat. I'm a sophomore at UNC studying Business Administration and Economics, and I'm working toward the buy-side — Private Equity or Private Credit.

I came at finance from the building side first, and I kept ending up more interested in the people who own the outcome than the ones advising on it. That's most of the story. Have a look around — the tabs walk through the work I've done, the people I've learned from, and where I'm trying to take it. Thanks for stopping by.

How I got here

None of this was a plan. It was one thing leading to the next, and each step making the previous one make more sense.

Troy, Michigan

Building things before I knew what to call it

All four years of high school I competed in an entrepreneurship competition, always on the business side — the market, the model, the money. What hooked me wasn't winning. It was that there was no answer in the back of the book. You made a case, someone pulled it apart, and you went back and made it better.

Spring 2026

My first look at a deal

I interned at a private holdings company buying small businesses. Cleaning up financials and sitting in on calls with brokers and lenders was the first time I saw the building instinct meet actual finance — someone was buying a company in order to run it, and the analysis existed to serve that.

Summer 2026

Advisory full-time, a platform on the side

I spent the summer full-time at an M&A advisory firm working buy-side mandates — sourcing targets, pitching which ones deserved attention, and handling the outreach that turns a name on a list into a meeting on a calendar. That's where I learned to communicate like a professional rather than a student.

Alongside it, I worked with an entrepreneur on bolt-on acquisitions for a platform he'd already bought. That one wasn't about volume — it was about building the framework underneath it: what made a target worth acquiring, and what made a partner worth having. One job taught me how the process runs, the other taught me how to decide what's worth putting into it.

On campus

Learning it with other people

I joined finance clubs that taught me to build a model and then defend what it says, spent time in consulting groups learning to structure a problem before reaching for a number, and helped start a club of my own when I noticed something missing on campus.

Most of what I know came from upperclassmen and mentors who had no particular reason to spend time on me and did anyway. That's the part I'd most like to pass on — I want to be the person doing that for someone two years behind me.

Where it points

Ownership, which is where it was always going

Looking back, the entrepreneurship and the investing are the same interest wearing different clothes. Both are about owning a decision: picking a direction, putting resources behind it, and living with what happens. Investing is the version where strategy and finance stop being separate subjects.

That's why the buy-side is the goal, and I'm recruiting for it directly. I want to end up somewhere I stay past the close — where the decision is mine to own and the results come back to me either way.

Where I am right now

I'm putting the work in. Three internships in, building models from a blank page rather than following someone else's, and treating the Economics side as something to actually use instead of a second line on a transcript.

I've started networking in earnest — reaching out, taking calls, and coming to them with real questions. Every one of those conversations has changed how I think about something, which is why I keep making them.

What I'm after now is structure and rigor: a clear plan for this cycle, and guidance from people who know the industry from the inside. That's the fastest way I know to turn effort into judgment, and I'd rather learn it from people who've done it.

Always happy to talk — about deals, markets, or anything above.

Internships

Three so far, and every one of them put me next to people who took real time to teach me. My resume has the bullet points — this is what the work was actually like.

Zol Capital

Corporate Development & Strategic Acquisitions Analyst

Miami, FL · Summer 2026

Finding bolt-ons for a platform we already owned

The firm had acquired a platform in endurance sports, and the work was figuring out which companies were worth bolting onto it. That meant researching a lot of small operators nobody writes about, estimating what they were worth when nothing was public, and building the framework that ranked them.

The same thinking carried into partnerships — which operators were worth working with even where an acquisition didn't make sense.

What I took from it: a scoring model can look finished and still be measuring the wrong thing. I found that out when the weights in one version didn't add up, which meant every score it had produced was quietly wrong.

Sellside Group

Junior M&A Analyst

Dallas, TX · Summer 2026

Two buy-side mandates, two clients

I worked buy-side searches for two different clients at once, finding businesses that fit what each of them wanted and running the outreach to owners. A lot of emails, a lot of dead ends, and every so often a conversation worth having.

Part of the job was setting up the meetings that came out of it and briefing the deal team on which names deserved their time.

What I took from it: sourcing is most of the job and almost nobody talks about it. A deal you never found is a deal you never do.

The Theofilis Group

Acquisition Intern

Cumming, GA · Spring 2026

One deal, alongside a first-time buyer

I worked a single deal with an entrepreneur searching for his first acquisition — cleaning up the financials, writing them up, and sitting in on calls with brokers and lenders as it moved toward closing.

Working one deal instead of many meant seeing the whole arc of it, including the parts that stall.

What I took from it: the numbers on the page are somebody's thirty years of work, and for the buyer they're everything he has. That changed how seriously I take getting them right.

Where I'm headed

I want to be on the buy-side — Private Equity or Private Credit. I respect advisory work and I'm recruiting for it, but the part that pulls at me is staying past the close. I'd rather own a decision to the end of the line and see the results of it, good or bad, than hand off the analysis and read about what happened later.

Private Equity

The closest thing to what I liked about building. You pick a company, take a view on what it could be, and then you're responsible for whether that view was right. The work doesn't end when the deal signs — that's roughly when it starts.

Private Credit

This came in sideways. I kept modeling the debt on deals and found the capital structure more interesting than the equity story sitting on top of it. Lending means being paid to think carefully about what goes wrong, which suits how I tend to read a business.

Markets, and why I added Economics

Honestly, I just find this genuinely interesting to follow. A business doesn't decide what it can borrow at, or whether customers feel like spending — the economy decides, and the business has to live in it. International markets are the part I follow most closely, because the same policy move lands completely differently depending on where you're standing.

Healthcare

This one started at home rather than in a classroom. My grandfather's experience gave my family a close look at how the system works, and it left me wanting to understand it properly rather than from the outside. It's also built strangely in a way I find fascinating: the person receiving the care, the one paying for it, and the one choosing it are almost never the same person.

Technology

Tech moves faster than anything else I follow — miss six months and the landscape has actually changed. That's exactly why I want to learn in it: a fast-moving space forces you to keep forming views instead of coasting on old ones. It's also where macro shows up quickest, since tech reprices first and hardest when rates move.

Still on the list

  • Secondaries — a whole market built on the gap between a mark and what someone will pay
  • Leveraged finance — how the debt actually gets structured, syndicated, and priced
  • How investors spend the years between buying something and selling it

How I actually follow it

Most mornings start with one of these. The habit I care about isn't the listening — it's taking a view off the back of it, writing down why, and then watching whether the market agrees with me. Being wrong in a way I can trace back to a bad assumption is worth more than being right by accident.

The best part is that my friends are into the same thing. We argue about rate paths and whether a run is real over lunch, someone pulls up a chart to prove a point, and I leave those conversations having rethought something. That back-and-forth is most of how I've learned anything.

Outside finance

The rest of the week, and most of the reason I like my life right now.

Bhangra with UNC Chalkaa

I'm a choreographer on the team, and the part I love most is that it takes us all over the country. We pack into cars and planes, show up in a city we've never been to, and get four minutes on a stage in front of people who have no reason to be nice to us. This season we took fourth at DDN Legends, the national championship of the South Asian collegiate circuit.

It's also the only thing I do where the feedback is instant. You can be certain a set works right up until two hundred people tell you it doesn't. The hours are absurd, which is maybe the most useful part — nothing else has taught me as much about showing up when it's inconvenient.

My friends, and the trips

Camping is my favorite thing we do, and Michigan is good for it — the dunes along the lake, and the Upper Peninsula when we have enough days to make the drive worth it. No signal, a fire, and people who knew me before any of this. It's the fastest way I know to remember that the recruiting calendar isn't the whole world.

We get further out when we can too. Cancún, and Miami before that — the kind of trips that take four months of group chat arguing to actually happen.

Some of these friends I've had since high school in Michigan and some I met three weeks into freshman year, and I'm lucky that it's hard to tell which is which.

Home

My parents and my younger brother are in Troy, Michigan, and I go back for every summer and every holiday. Finance takes up most of my calendar and I like that it does — but the reason I'm reaching for any of this is in these photos. My family is why coming to UNC felt like a stretch worth making, and why I'd like to make something real out of it.

I get to work on things I find interesting with people I actually like. I know that isn't the default, and I'm not planning to get used to it.
